text:
“Marie, she is such a delight!” she said. “How well she understands children. It is as though she sees only their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitenka began to be capricious...”

“Oh, how like his father he is,” Pierre interrupted.

Natasha understood why he had made this remark about Mitenka’s resemblance to Nikolai: the recollection of his dispute with his brother-in-law was unpleasant to him, and he wanted to know Natasha’s opinion of it.

“Nikolenka has this weakness: if something is not accepted by everyone, he will not agree to it for anything. But I understand that what you particularly value is opening up a career,” she said, repeating words Pierre had once spoken.

“No, the main thing,” said Pierre, “is that for Nikolai, thoughts and reasoning are an amusement, almost a way of passing the time. There he is, assembling a library, and he has made it a rule not to buy a new book before he has read the one he bought—Sismondi, and Rousseau, and Montesquieu,” Pierre added with a smile. “You know, after all, how I...” he began, intending to soften his words; but Natasha interrupted him, making it clear that this was unnecessary.

“So you say that for him thoughts are an amusement...”

“Yes, while for me everything else is an amusement. All the time I was in Petersburg, I saw everyone as though in a dream. When a thought occupies me, everything else is an amusement.”

“Oh, what a pity I did not see you greeting the children,” said Natasha. “Which one was happiest of all? Liza, surely?”

“Yes,” said Pierre, and he continued with what occupied him. “Nikolai says we must not think. But I cannot help it. Not to mention that in Petersburg I felt—I can tell you this—that without me the whole thing was falling apart, everyone was pulling in a different direction. But I managed to unite them all, and then my idea is so simple and clear. You see, I am not saying that we must oppose this person or that person. We may be mistaken. What I say is: let those who love goodness join hands, and let there be one banner—active virtue. Prince Sergei is a splendid man and intelligent.”

Natasha would not have doubted that Pierre’s idea was a great idea, but one thing troubled her. It was that he was her husband. “Can such an important and necessary man for society be at the same time my husband? Why did it happen this way?” She wanted to express this doubt to him. “Who are the people who could decide whether he really is so much cleverer than everyone else?” she asked herself, going over in her imagination those people whom Pierre held in very high esteem. Judging by his stories, there was no one in the whole world whom he respected as much as Platon Karataev.

“Do you know what I am thinking about?” she said. “About Platon Karataev. What about him? Would he approve of you now?”

Pierre was not at all surprised by the question. He understood the course of his wife’s thoughts.

“Platon Karataev?” he said, and grew thoughtful, evidently making a sincere effort to imagine Karataev’s judgment on the matter. “He would not have understood, though perhaps he might have approved.”

“I love you terribly!” Natasha said suddenly. “Terribly. Terribly!”

“No, he would not have approved,” said Pierre after thinking. “What he would have approved of is our family life. He so wished to see seemliness, happiness, and tranquility in everything, and I would proudly have shown him the two of us. Now, you speak of separation. But you would not believe what a special feeling I have for you after a separation...”

“Oh, there you go again...” Natasha began.

“No, not that. I never stop loving you. And it is impossible to love you more; but this is something special... Well, yes...” He did not finish, because their eyes met and said the rest.

“What nonsense,” Natasha said suddenly, “this honeymoon and the idea that the greatest happiness is at the beginning. On the contrary, now is the best time. If only you did not go away. Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And I was always to blame. Always me. And I do not even remember what we quarreled about.”

“Always about the same thing,” said Pierre with a smile, “jeal—”

“Do not say it; I cannot bear it,” Natasha cried out. And a cold, angry gleam appeared in her eyes. “Did you see her?” she added after a pause.

“No, and even if I had seen her, I would not have recognized her.”

They were silent.

“Oh, do you know? When you were speaking in the study, I was looking at you,” Natasha began, evidently trying to drive away the cloud that had come over them. “You are as like him as two drops of water, like the boy.” (That was what she called her son.) “Oh, it is time to go to him... My milk has come... And I am sorry to leave.”

They were silent for several seconds. Then suddenly, at the same moment, they turned toward each other and began to say something. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm; Natasha, with a quiet, happy smile. Having spoken at once, they both stopped, each yielding to the other.

“No, what were you going to say? Speak, speak.”

“No, you say it; mine was only nonsense,” said Natasha.

Pierre said what he had begun to say. It was a continuation of his self-satisfied reasoning about his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he had been called upon to give a new direction to all of Russian society and to the whole world.

“I only wanted to say that all thoughts that have enormous consequences are always simple. My whole idea is that if vicious people are bound together and constitute a force, then honest people need only do the same thing. It is so simple.”

“Yes.”

“And what did you want to say?”

“Mine was only nonsense.”

“No, tell me anyway.”

“Oh, nothing, a trifle,” said Natasha, her smile growing still more radiant. “I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today the nurse came up to take him from me, and he laughed, screwed up his eyes, and pressed himself against me—he must have thought he was hiding. Terribly sweet. There, he is crying. Well, goodbye!” And she left the room.

At the same time, downstairs, in the part of the house occupied by little Nikolinka Bolkonsky, a sanctuary lamp was burning in his bedroom as always (the boy was afraid of the dark, and they had been unable to cure him of this failing). Dessalles was asleep, propped high on his four pillows, and his Roman nose was producing steady sounds of snoring. Nikolinka, who had just awakened, sat on his bed in a cold sweat, his eyes wide open, staring straight ahead. A terrible dream had awakened him. In his dream he had seen himself and Pierre wearing helmets like those depicted in the edition of Plutarch. He and Uncle Pierre were marching at the head of an enormous army. This army consisted of white, slanting lines that filled the air like the strands of gossamer that float in autumn and that Dessalles called the Virgin’s thread. Ahead of them was glory, like those same strands, only somewhat denser. They—he and Pierre—were borne lightly and joyfully closer and closer to their goal. Suddenly the strands that propelled them began to weaken and become entangled; the going became difficult. And Uncle Nikolai Ilyich stopped before them in a menacing and stern pose.
